target.title: Movement Detection of Tongue and Related Body Parts Using IR-UWB Radar

read.pdf: Figs. 1–3 and Table I; all five pages, including references, visually checked

entries.text: The study explores chin-directed IR-UWB sensing as a way to detect otherwise invisible tongue movement and related-body-part movement.
entries.condition: Feasibility experiment; antennas pointed toward the participant's chin; closed-mouth rest versus tongue-tip palate touch.
entries.quote: radar, whose antennas are pointed toward the user’s chin.

entries.text: The sensing setup used an IR-UWB radar module, an LNA evaluation board, sinuous antennas, and a dielectric lens.
entries.condition: Single experimental hardware setup shown in Fig. 1.

entries.text: The participant's chin was positioned approximately 5–10 cm above the radar antenna.
entries.condition: Experimental chin-directed IR-UWB setup; participants sat during recording.
entries.quote: Participants were asked to sit and locate their chin approximately 5–10 cm above the radar antenna.

entries.text: Four participants took part: two male and two female.
entries.condition: The evaluation is reported separately for each participant; no participant-held-out test is described.
entries.quote: In total, four participants, including two males and two females, participated in the experiment.

entries.text: P1 was male and an author; P2 was male; P3 and P4 were female.
entries.condition: The table's participant IDs refer to these four participants; P1's author status is disclosed.
entries.quote: One of the male participants was one of the authors of this study.

entries.text: The two instructed classes were tongue resting on the mouth floor and tongue-tip contact with the palate followed by return to rest; the mouth was closed so the tongue was invisible.
entries.condition: Participants were asked to keep the rest of the body as still as possible; this is binary state detection, not lexical speech recognition.
entries.quote: An experiment was conducted to distinguish between the states of rest and movement of the tongue while the participants closed their mouths.

entries.text: Participants repeated each of the two states twenty times, yielding 40 frame sets per participant.
entries.condition: Two states; 40 total frame sets for each participant; state timing was manually started and stopped.

entries.text: Each state recording lasted approximately 1–3 seconds, regardless of state.
entries.condition: Manual state recording in the closed-mouth, chin-directed radar experiment.
entries.quote: The data measurement period was approximately 1–3 s regardless of the state.

entries.text: Recording start and finish for each state were manually triggered with a GUI button; the paper does not describe automatic segmentation or continuous online operation.
entries.condition: Experimental acquisition and state-window definition.
entries.quote:
The starting and ﬁnishing of measuring of each state was decided by manually clicking
graphic user interface button on computer screen.

entries.text: Received pulses were merged into frames using the manufacturer's normalization method; the specific normalization algorithm or settings are not given.
entries.condition: Radar front-end preprocessing before the 256-point frame representation.

entries.text: Each radar frame contained 256 fast-time samples, with each index representing distance from the radar.
entries.condition: A frame set is represented as T-by-256; frame samples are manufacturer-normalized signal values.

entries.text: The reported signal-strength value at each discrete fast-time index ranged from 0 to 100.
entries.condition: Per fast-time index of each manufacturer-normalized radar frame.

entries.text: The radar acquired approximately 200 frames per second.
entries.condition: IR-UWB radar during each participant's state recording.

entries.text: Each frame set is a T-by-256 matrix of T acquired frames; the paper's example maps 200 frames/s over 2 s to T = 400.
entries.condition: Illustrative example only, not a fixed recording length; actual recordings lasted approximately 1–3 s.

entries.text: Feature extraction concatenated a frame set, calculated a sliding-window RMS envelope using a 400-length window, then downsampled and mean-centered it to length T/4.
entries.condition: Applied to each frame set before classification; no additional feature scaling is described.
entries.quote: To detect the envelope, we generated a 400-length sliding window on the concatenated data and calculated a root mean square (RMS) value of the data within each window.

entries.text: The extracted envelope was downsampled to length T/4 and mean-subtracted to remove its DC offset.
entries.condition: Proposed feature pipeline; T is the acquired-frame count in the frame set.

entries.text: The proposed classifier was a five-state left-to-right HMM with one single-mixture Gaussian emission model per state.
entries.condition: Two class-specific GMM-HMMs were used, one for state 1 and one for state 2; variable-length features were passed without length-fixing.
entries.quote: In detail, we used a ﬁve-state left-to-right HMM and the emission probability per state was modeled with a single mixture Gaussian.

entries.text: The GMM-HMM training used separate features from state-1 and state-2 frame sets to train one model for each class.
entries.condition: Within each LOOCV fold, models were trained on the 39 non-test frame sets for that participant.

entries.text: At classification time the test frame set was assigned to whichever of the state-1 or state-2 GMM-HMMs gave the larger probability.
entries.condition: Two state-specific models; no vocabulary decoder or language model is described.

entries.text: The paper describes Shin and Seo's short-template CLEAN as outperforming conventional CLEAN in a prior IR-UWB 10-word classification task.
entries.condition: Prior-work description attributed to reference [46], not a result of the present binary-state experiment.

entries.text: The cited prior CLEAN comparison involved a 10-word classification task using IR-UWB radar.
entries.unit: words in the prior classification task
entries.condition: Prior work [46]; this is not the vocabulary size or task evaluated in the current paper.

entries.text: The CLEAN baselines extracted target distance and reflected-pulse strength features per frame and classified frame sets by MD-DTW nearest distance; the paper also applied signal-averaging clutter reduction.
entries.condition: Conventional CLEAN + MD-DTW and short-template CLEAN + MD-DTW; baseline descriptions refer to [46].
entries.quote:
The classiﬁcation was performed by utilizing the multidimensional dynamic time warping (MD-DTW) algo-
rithm, which provides the distance between two frame sets based on their multidimensional features.

entries.text: The evaluation used participant-specific leave-one-out cross-validation across 40 frame sets: one test set and the other 39 for training in each fold.
entries.condition: Repeated for each participant and for each of the three methods; test and training sets are from the same participant.
entries.quote: To apply LOOCV , each of the 40 frame sets was used for the test and the other 39 frame sets were used for training.

entries.text: The system output is a binary state label, state 1 or state 2, rather than a word or sentence.
entries.condition: State 1 is tongue rest; state 2 is tongue-tip palate contact and return to rest; no lexical decoding is reported.

entries.text: Per-participant accuracy was the number of correctly classified frame sets divided by 40 and multiplied by 100.
entries.condition: Each participant has 40 frame sets; reported accuracies are participant-specific LOOCV results.

entries.text: The authors claim that the proposed feature-extraction/GMM-HMM method had higher accuracy than either CLEAN-based method for every participant.
entries.condition: Comparison is limited to the three methods in Table I and the four participants under participant-specific LOOCV.
entries.quote: all the individual classiﬁcation results based on the proposed method showed higher accuracy than any other method-based result.

entries.text: The paper reports a minimum proposed-method classification accuracy of 90% across four individual participants.
entries.condition: Proposed feature extraction + GMM-HMM; closed-mouth rest versus palate-touch movement; chin-directed IR-UWB with chin approximately 5–10 cm above the antenna; each participant evaluated by LOOCV on their 40 frame sets (20 repetitions/state; 1 test and 39 training per fold); binary state classification, no lexical vocabulary or language model; session boundaries/split and random seed are not reported; no speaker-held-out evaluation.

entries.text: The authors conclude that chin-directed IR-UWB can detect invisible tongue and related-body-part movement when suitable features and classifiers are used.
entries.condition: The evidence is a four-participant binary rest/palate-touch feasibility experiment, not word recognition.
entries.quote: Therefore, we conclude that an IR-UWB radar has the capability to detect the movement of invisible tongue and its related body parts if proper features and classiﬁcation algorithms are applied.

entries.text: The authors observed that throat muscles moved together with tongue movement and state that the radar detects tongue and related-body-part movement simultaneously; the signal is therefore not shown to be tongue-specific.
entries.condition: No independent tongue-motion measurement or separation of tongue from hyoid/suprahyoid motion is reported.
entries.quote: Thus, the movement of tongue and its related body parts is detected simultaneously by an IR-UWB radar.

entries.text: The proposed contribution is the feature-extraction algorithm paired with a conventional GMM-HMM classifier, rather than a novel HMM architecture.
entries.condition: The authors explicitly characterize the GMM-HMM as conventional and the feature extraction algorithm as proposed.
entries.quote: We proposed a feature extraction algorithm, and used a conventional Gaussian mixture model–hidden Markov model (GMM–HMM) [51] for the classiﬁcation task.

entries.text: The authors explain that CLEAN features track the strongest arbitrary target and may omit movement information from the tongue and related body parts.
entries.condition: Authors' explanation for the lower CLEAN-baseline results in this experiment.

entries.text: The authors report greater fluctuation in the proposed feature for the moving/palate-touch state than the resting state.
entries.condition: Illustrative features in Fig. 3, not an additional quantitative result.

questions.q: Does the experiment establish tongue-specific sensing, or does it detect movement correlated with tongue action?
questions.answer: The authors report simultaneous movement of throat muscles and say tongue and related-body-part movement are detected together; they provide no independent reference measurement to isolate tongue motion.

questions.q: Do the reported accuracies establish generalization to unseen speakers or sessions?
questions.answer: No. The evaluation is LOOCV within each participant's 40 frame sets, and no participant-held-out or session-held-out test is reported.

questions.q: Is this a silent-speech recognition result, and what does the reported minimum accuracy measure?
questions.answer: It measures binary classification of tongue-rest versus tongue-tip palate-touch frame sets, not recognition of words or sentences; the proposed method's lowest participant result is 90%.

questions.q: How strong is the superiority claim over the CLEAN baselines?
questions.answer: The proposed method exceeds both evaluated baselines for all four participants in Table I, but no confidence intervals, significance tests, or run-to-run variability are reported.

questions.q: Where did the 2016 IR-UWB study place the radar, and did it already detect motion from the radar signal?
questions.answer: Reader run (free model) produced no output within the time limit; the writer grepped the specific passages of doi-10.3390-s16111812: lips and jaw at 10-16 cm; variance-based motion detection; nearest-echo CLEAN. Ferreira 2022 dropped from the review.
